title: Nearly Half of Indian Doctors Use AI in Practice, Yet 69% Say They Want to Quit Medicine
excerpt: A striking paradox in Indian healthcare: doctors are embracing technology faster than almost any other profession, but burnout, low pay, and systemic dysfunction are driving a mass exodus urge.
body:
• A recent survey found that 49% of Indian doctors are using AI tools in clinical practice — one of the highest adoption rates globally
  • Despite this technological embrace, 69% of surveyed doctors expressed a desire to leave the medical profession entirely
  • Key drivers of disillusionment include long working hours, inadequate compensation, violence against healthcare workers, and bureaucratic burdens
  • The paradox highlights a healthcare system that is modernizing its tools while failing to address the human cost of practicing medicine in India

Nearly half of India's doctors have integrated artificial intelligence into their daily practice — using AI for diagnostic support, medical imaging analysis, and treatment planning at rates that rival or exceed their counterparts in developed nations. Yet a staggering 69% of these same doctors say they want to quit medicine altogether.

The AI Adoption Surge

The 49% AI adoption figure, drawn from a recent survey of Indian physicians, reflects a profession that has embraced technology with unusual speed. AI-powered tools are being used for everything from reading radiology scans and pathology slides to generating differential diagnoses and drafting clinical notes.

Part of the explanation is practical necessity: India's doctor-to-patient ratio remains far below WHO recommendations, and AI tools help physicians manage crushing patient volumes that would be considered unsafe in most Western healthcare systems. When you're seeing 80-100 patients a day, any tool that speeds up diagnosis or documentation isn't a luxury — it's survival.

Why They Want to Leave

The 69% quit-intention figure is the more alarming statistic, and it points to problems that no algorithm can solve. Indian doctors consistently cite long working hours — 60-80 hours per week is common for hospital-based physicians — inadequate compensation relative to their training, violence from frustrated patients and families, and suffocating administrative burdens.

Public hospital doctors in India earn a fraction of what private practitioners make, yet face the heaviest caseloads. Junior doctors and residents regularly work 36-hour shifts. And the epidemic of violence against healthcare workers — physical assaults by patients' relatives unhappy with outcomes — has created a pervasive sense of insecurity that technology cannot address.

The Diaspora Connection

These findings echo the same pressures that have driven generations of Indian medical graduates abroad. The US, UK, Canada, and Gulf countries are home to hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin physicians who cite not just better pay but better working conditions, institutional support, and physical safety as reasons they left.

For NRI doctors watching from abroad, the survey data validates their decision while raising uncomfortable questions about the system they left behind. India's healthcare infrastructure is modernizing at the surface — AI adoption, telemedicine expansion, new hospital chains — while the foundational problems of physician burnout, inadequate staffing, and workplace safety remain largely unaddressed.

The paradox is stark: India is producing doctors who are savvy enough to adopt cutting-edge AI tools, then creating conditions so hostile that most of them want to stop being doctors.
